passages.title: Learning the River's Language
passages.text:
The first time I paddled the Clearwater River with my aunt Rosa, I spent most of the trip staring at the bow of my kayak. Rosa, {{1|who has guided rafting trips for twenty years}} kept telling me to look up. "The river is talking," she said. "You just have to learn {{2|it's}} language."

Over the next summer, I began to understand what she meant. Between two submerged rocks {{3|lies}} the safest channel, marked by a smooth V pointing downstream. A V pointing upstream warns of a hidden boulder. Waves that curl back on themselves, called holes, can trap a {{4|boat, even}} a skilled paddler avoids them. Reading these signs {{5|quick}} became a habit; by August I was calling out hazards before Rosa did.

{{6|Kayaks can be made of plastic, fiberglass, or wood.}} Rosa taught me to check the gauge reports each morning, because a river that rises a foot overnight {{7|can, in a very short amount of time, transform}} a gentle stretch into a dangerous one. She kept a notebook of water levels going back a decade, and she could predict, almost to the hour, when the spring melt would peak.

On my last trip of the season, Rosa let me lead. I chose our line through every rapid, and twice I steered us around holes {{8|that were near the left bank.}} {{9|Watching me pick a line through the last rapid, a grin spread across Rosa's face.}} At the take-out, she handed me her notebook. "You'll need this more than I will," she said. {{10|I still have it.}} {{11|Its pages are filled with numbers, and in every one I can hear the river talking.}}

passages.title: The Last Sign Painter in Calder
passages.genre: profile (original; Calder and Marrow are invented)
passages.text:
In the river town of Calder, nearly every storefront sign was painted by hand, and most of them {{1|was}} painted by the same woman. For forty years, Edith Marrow climbed ladders with a {{2|brush a can of enamel, and a steady hand}}, lettering the names of bakeries, barbershops, and hardware stores {{3|onto there}} windows and walls.

Marrow learned the trade from her father, who {{4|had painted signs}} for the town since before she was born. {{5|He taught her to mix colors, to space letters by eye, and that a sign should be read from across the street.}} She practiced on scrap boards in the garage, painting the alphabet hundreds of times until her strokes were {{6|identical; even}} her father could not tell them from his own.

When vinyl lettering machines arrived in the 1990s, many of Marrow's customers switched. The machines were faster and {{7|cheaper, however,}} the stickers they produced {{8|got kind of messed up}} within a few years. One by one, the shop owners came back. "A machine can make a letter," one barber told a reporter, "but it can't make a sign."

Today Marrow is in her seventies and no longer climbs ladders. {{9|Still, she enjoys gardening and reading in her spare time.}} {{10|Her students, many of whom are young and in their twenties,}} say they come for the craft but stay for the patience it teaches.

passages.title: Mapping the Dark
passages.text:
When most people imagine cave exploration, they picture squeezing through tight passages in search {{1|for}} undiscovered chambers. The work that occupies most cavers, however, is slower and less glamorous: making maps. {{2|Without a map, a cave that has been explored is, for practical purposes, a cave that has been lost.}}

A survey team usually has three members. The first sets a station—a small numbered marker—at a point the others can see. {{3|The second, who holds a laser rangefinder, measures}} the distance to the station, while the third reads the compass bearing and the slope. {{4|Each of these numbers are recorded}} in a waterproof notebook, along with a sketch of the passage's walls.

[1] Back on the surface, the numbers become a map. [2] A single misread digit can send that path through solid rock. [3] Software converts each set of measurements into a line segment, and the segments, joined end to end, trace the cave's path. [4] For this reason, many teams measure every leg twice, once in each direction.

The work is slow. A team might survey only a few hundred meters in a long day, {{5|and the rangefinders run on rechargeable batteries}}. {{6|Yet}} cavers keep at it, {{7|year after year, decade after decade, for many years}}, because a good map is the one discovery that lasts: {{8|its useful}} to every caver, scientist, and rescue team that enters the cave afterward. {{9|Whom}} else would bother to do it?

passages.text:
The letters arrived in a shoebox the summer after my grandmother died: forty-three of them, written in Portuguese to her sister in the Azores and returned to our family after the {{1|sisters'}} deaths. I had studied Portuguese for two years in high school, and I assumed that would be enough. It was not.

My grandmother wrote the way she talked, in long sentences full of village nicknames and expressions I could not find in any dictionary. {{2|For example,}} she called the town's priest "the Rooster," and she described a hard winter as "a winter with teeth." Some pages took me an entire evening. On one, she had copied a few lines by the Portuguese {{3|poet, Fernando Pessoa,}} into the margin, and next to them she had written a single word {{4|that, I eventually translated as}} "exactly."

I began keeping a notebook of the phrases I could not translate, and by the end of the summer it held more than two hundred entries. At first, the notebook felt like a list of failures. Gradually it became something else: a record of {{5|the way, my grandmother saw}} the world, one stubborn phrase at a time. {{6|The notebook had cost three dollars at a drugstore.}}

I still cannot read Portuguese {{7|fluently. I can}}, however, recognize my grandmother's voice in it, {{8|which took me most of a long summer}}. Last month I {{9|lended}} the notebook to my cousin, who is starting on the letters herself.

passages.title: The Seed Library
passages.text:
When the Hollins Branch Library began lending seeds in 2019, {{1|it's}} staff expected only a few gardeners to take an interest. Instead, the first {{2|three hundred packets—tomatoes, beans, and squash, were}} gone within a week. Borrowers take seeds in the spring, grow the plants over the summer, and return a portion of the new seeds in the fall, so the collection renews itself. The program costs almost nothing to run: donated envelopes, a card catalog rescued from the basement, and a few hours of volunteer time each week.

The idea is not new. Farmers have saved and traded seeds for thousands of years, and the program's founder, {{3|librarian, Dana Whitfield,}} learned the practice from her grandmother. {{4|Her grandmother also kept bees and sold the honey at a roadside stand.}} What has changed is the scale. Today the collection holds more than two hundred varieties, many of them adapted over generations to the region's short summers and heavy clay soil. Tomatoes grown from the library's seeds often ripen two weeks earlier than {{5|commercial packets}}.

In theory, every borrower returns seeds each fall. {{6|In practice,}} about a third never do, and others return seeds from squash that cross-pollinated with a neighbor's plants, producing gourds no one can eat. The staff responded with a simple {{7|rule, seeds}} from squash must now come back labeled with the address of the garden where they grew. If every borrower {{8|will return}} seeds, Whitfield says, the collection would double each year.

Even so, the variety of beans that borrowers have brought back over the years {{9|have}} surprised her. Some of those beans, a speckled variety from a farm that closed decades ago, exist nowhere else. Whitfield keeps a jar of them on her desk, and she lends them only to gardeners who promise to bring twice as many back.

passages.title: The Night Ferry
passages.text:
For ninety years, a ferry has crossed the harbor between Port Ellery and Gull Island every night at eleven. The boat itself {{1|had changed}} several times; the current one, the blue-hulled {{2|Marguerite,}} entered service in 1998. Its schedule, however, has not. Riders say the night ferry is as dependable as the tide. On a calm night the crossing takes twenty-two minutes, and the lights of Gull Island grow from a faint smudge into a row of windows along the pier.

Most of the late-night passengers are workers. {{3|Among them is}} nurses finishing hospital shifts, cooks from the restaurants along the waterfront, and a baker {{4|on who}} the island depends for its morning bread. The captain, Lou Petrakis, knows most of them by name. He keeps a thermos of coffee in the wheelhouse for regulars and a box of spare gloves for anyone who forgets a pair in winter.

Running a ferry at night is harder than {{5|daytime}}. Fog rolls in without warning, and the harbor's buoys, {{6|which are only dimly lit at night when it is dark}}, can be hard to see. {{7|For this reason,}} Petrakis has memorized the channel so thoroughly that he says he could steer it with his eyes closed, though he has never tried.

Last spring the city proposed ending the night run to save money. More than two thousand residents signed a petition against the plan, and the nurses' union {{8|argued, that}} cutting the route would leave hospital workers with no way home after late shifts. At a public hearing, the baker brought a loaf of bread for every member of the council. In June the city {{9|reversed course}}. {{10|The ferry still leaves at eleven.}}

passages.title: The Piano Doctor
passages.text:
Ines Ortega's workshop sits above a laundromat on Delancey Street, and on most days the hum of the dryers below {{1|mixes}} with the sound of a single note being struck over and over. Ortega restores old pianos{{2|; a}} trade she learned from her uncle in Guadalajara. Most of the instruments that reach her have spent decades in church basements or in the living rooms of families who no longer play them.

Restoring a piano is slow work. Each of the eighty-eight keys must be removed and cleaned and must have {{3|their}} felt replaced, and the hammers that strike the strings often need to be reshaped by hand. {{4|Working with a small file, the felt on each hammer is shaved}} until it strikes the string at exactly the right angle. A full restoration can take Ortega three months, and she tunes each instrument several times before it leaves the shop, since new felt and freshly cleaned keys take weeks to settle.

Not every piano is worth saving. Some have cracked soundboards or warped frames, and repairing them would cost more than the instrument is worth. {{5|Nevertheless,}} Ortega rarely turns a piano away. She salvages {{6|certain useful items}} from the ones she cannot fix and uses them to repair others.

Humidity has a strong {{7|affect}} on a piano's wooden parts, so Ortega {{8|keeps her workshop at a steady temperature and runs a dehumidifier, and she checks}} the moisture level twice a day.

Last spring a church that had sold its piano decades earlier asked Ortega to find one like it. She found the original instead{{9|. In pieces,}} in her own storeroom. It took her four months to restore, and when the choir heard it again, several members said it sounded exactly as they remembered.

passages.title: Counting Sea Stars
passages.text:
Twice a month, during the lowest tides, a group of volunteers gathers on the rocks below Point Harlan with clipboards and measuring tapes. They are counting sea stars{{1|, the}} task is slower than it sounds. Each animal must be found, measured, and checked for signs of the wasting disease that killed millions of sea stars along the Pacific coast beginning in 2013.

The survey was started by Lena Ashby, a marine biologist {{2|which}} teaches at the community college nearby. When the disease first appeared, she realized that no one had kept careful records of how many sea stars lived at the point before the outbreak. {{3|Without those numbers, it was impossible to say how much had been lost.}} She resolved that if another outbreak came, there would be a baseline.

The volunteers range from retirees to high school students. Most had never {{4|seen, a sea star}} up close before joining, and Ashby trains them in a single afternoon. Two people looking at the same pool, she has found, rarely count exactly the same number of animals. {{5|For this reason,}} she insists that every count be checked by a second person.

The work has already paid off. In 2021, the volunteers noticed young sea stars in pools where none had been seen for years. Because the survey had begun well before the recovery, Ashby had the numbers to measure it. By the time she published her report in 2023, the number of juveniles {{6|has tripled}} since the first sightings{{7|. A}} finding she later shared with researchers at three universities.

Ashby says the most important quality in a volunteer is not expertise but {{8|patience and the patient ability to wait calmly}}. The {{9|volunteers}} records now fill eleven binders, and she hopes they will someday make dull reading: a long, uneventful list of healthy sea stars.

passages.title: The First Forecasts
passages.text:
In August 1861, readers of The Times in London found something new in their newspaper: a forecast of the next day's weather. The prediction was the work of Robert FitzRoy, a naval officer who had once commanded HMS Beagle on Charles Darwin's famous voyage. FitzRoy had grown alarmed by the {{1|amount of}} ships lost in storms along the British coast, and he believed that many could be saved if sailors had some warning. A storm in 1859 that sank more than a hundred vessels, including a passenger ship off the coast of Wales, convinced him that the problem could no longer be ignored.

FitzRoy's method relied on a newer technology: the telegraph. Each morning, observers at stations around the coast sent {{2|they're}} readings of air pressure, temperature, and wind to London. By comparing the readings, FitzRoy could see a storm approaching before it arrived. He called his predictions "forecasts," {{3|a word that he chose and selected because}} it suggested a reasoned estimate rather than a prophecy. He also arranged for warning signals, made of canvas cones and drums, to be hoisted at harbors when a gale was expected.

The forecasts were popular with the public, but scientists {{4|were less impressed, many of them}} dismissed FitzRoy's work as guesswork. {{5|In contrast,}} the forecasts were often wrong, and newspapers sometimes printed the errors with amusement. FitzRoy, who took the criticism personally, worked {{6|ceaselessly, and tirelessly}} to improve them.

After FitzRoy's death in 1865, the forecasts were halted. Ships' captains and ordinary readers {{7|complained, and}} within two years storm warnings had returned; printed daily forecasts followed in 1879. {{8|Today, weather forecasts are produced by computer models that process millions of observations every day.}} The basic idea, however, remains {{9|FitzRoys gather}} observations from many places at once and look for the pattern they make together.

passages.title: The Millbrook Carousel
passages.text:
When the town of Millbrook bought its carousel in 1921, the ride {{1|costed}} more than the town's new fire truck. For decades it turned every summer in Riverside Park, its forty-two wooden horses carved by hand and {{2|it's}} brass poles polished each spring by volunteers. Children chose their favorite horses by name, and some families took the same horses year after year, as if they owned them.

By 1990, however, the carousel had fallen silent. Its motor {{3|had broke}}, several horses had cracked, and the town could not afford repairs. A plan to sell the horses to a collector was proposed twice and voted down twice. The horses were stored in a barn {{4|where they waited, unused and idle, for nearly twenty years without being used}}.

In 2009 a retired shop teacher named Walter Okafor offered to restore them. He had never carved a horse, {{5|but he}} had spent forty years teaching students to work with wood. {{6|Working in his garage, the horses were repaired by Okafor one at a time.}} He replaced missing ears and tails, filled cracks with matching wood, and {{7|repainting}} each horse in the colors shown in a 1925 photograph.

The work took six years, partly because Okafor insisted on using only wood from trees that had fallen naturally in the county. {{8|Okafor did not finish the job alone, though.}} Volunteers raised money for a new motor, and a local electrician rewired the ride without charge. {{9|In contrast,}} in the summer of 2015, the carousel reopened, and more than two thousand people lined up to ride it. {{10|Tickets cost two dollars, and the line stretched past the park's main gate.}}

passages.title: The Shortcut
passages.text:
The summer I turned sixteen, I took a job sweeping floors at Hanley & Daughters, a bookbindery that had operated on Water Street since 1934. The shop {{1|smelled of glue, leather, and old paper,}} and the radio on the workbench played the same baseball station all day. {{2|Mrs. Hanley was the owner, she}} had been binding books in that room for almost fifty years.

For the first few weeks, I only swept and watched. Mrs. Hanley folded large printed sheets into sections called signatures, sewed the signatures together along their spines, and {{3|then she glued}} each sewn block into a cover. Each of the hundreds of books on her shelves {{4|were}} sewn by hand. She never used the machine that sat in the corner, {{5|which she called "the shortcut."}}

In August, she finally let me bind a book of my own. My first attempt was a disaster. The stitches were uneven, the spine leaned to one side, and the cover {{6|wouldn't hardly}} close. I expected her to drop it in the scrap bin. {{7|Nevertheless,}} Mrs. Hanley studied it for a long time, turning it over in her hands, before she gave it back to me. "Now make one with {{8|less}} knots," she said.

I made eleven more books before school started again. {{9|}} Each one was a little better than the last. By the twelfth, the stitches were even, the spine was straight, and the cover closed {{10|flatly and evenly without any gaps.}} Mrs. Hanley put that book on the shelf beside her own, and it is still there today.

passages.title: Moving the Lighthouse
passages.text:
When it was completed in 1870, the brick lighthouse on the barrier island stood about 1,500 feet from the ocean. Over the next century, storms and the slow westward drift of the island {{1|carried the shoreline so close, that waves}} sometimes washed against the tower's base. By the 1990s, engineers warned that a single severe hurricane {{2|could of toppled}} it.

Officials considered several ways to protect the lighthouse. A stronger seawall could shield the tower {{3|for a time, but it}} would also speed the erosion of nearby beaches. {{4|Similarly, the National Park Service chose a bolder plan:}} lifting the brick tower off its foundation and rolling it inland.

The move was {{5|slow with design}}. Workers cut the tower free from its foundation, slid steel beams beneath it, and raised it with hydraulic jacks. Then, a few feet at a time, they pushed it along a track of steel rails while engineers {{6|monitor}} sensors that would warn them if it began to lean. After twenty-three days, the lighthouse {{7|arrived to}} its new site, about half a mile from the sea.

Not everyone had supported the move. Some critics predicted that the old bricks would crack apart; others argued that a lighthouse belongs beside the water and {{8|it would lose its meaning}} anywhere else. {{9|The tower survived the trip without a single crack.}} Today, visitors who climb to the top can look out over the ocean{{10|, which}} is now a comfortable distance away.

passages.title: Recipes Worth Keeping
passages.text:
Last fall, our history teacher, Ms. Ito, asked each pair of students in our class to interview a resident of the senior center across the street and write down one family recipe for a class cookbook. She assigned my partner and {{1|I}} to Mr. Okoye, a retired engineer who had moved to the city from Nigeria fifty years earlier.

Each week we {{2|visit}} the center after school. Mr. Okoye was more willing to talk about his childhood {{3|then}} about cooking, and for the first two visits we wrote down only stories. We listened {{4|careful}}, though, and the stories turned out to matter. His recipe for pepper soup{{5|—which}} he had never written down, was one his mother had taught him in a kitchen with no measuring cups, and he described every ingredient by the size of a hand or the color of a broth.

[1] The hardest part of the project was turning those descriptions into measurements. [2] Then we checked each batch with him. [3] We cooked the soup three times in the school's kitchen, adjusting the pepper each time. [4] On the third try, he tasted it, closed his eyes, and said only, "Yes." {{6|}}

Of the two Nigerian recipes in the cookbook, his turned out to be {{7|the most}} popular with the other residents. The finished book contained recipes from four {{8|countries: Mexico,}} Nigeria, Japan, and Poland. The {{9|affect}} of the project surprised all of us. Several residents asked for extra copies to send to their grandchildren, and Mr. Okoye now cooks pepper soup for the center's monthly dinner.

passages.title: Setting the Shadow Straight
passages.text:
For as long as anyone at Harlow Middle School could remember, a stone sundial had stood in the courtyard outside the library, and for just as long, it had been useless. Its bronze pointer, called a gnomon, had been bent sideways years earlier{{1|—probably by a falling branch, and}} its shadow pointed nowhere near the right hour.

Last spring our science club decided to fix it. The club had less than forty dollars in {{2|their}} account, so we asked the hardware store on Main Street for help. The owner {{3|was nice about it and helped us out a lot}}, and our adviser, Ms. Varga, found an old diagram of the dial in the school archives.

[1] The first problem was the angle. [2] For our town, that angle is about 42 degrees. [3] For the shadow to keep accurate time, the gnomon's slanted edge must point toward the North Star. [4] That means the edge has to rise from the dial at an angle equal to the latitude of the place where the sundial stands. [5] To set the angle, we {{4|needed: a protractor,}} a level, and a magnetic compass. {{5|}}

{{6|Ms. Varga had once taught science in Arizona.}} A magnetic compass points to magnetic north, which in our area lies more than ten degrees away from true north. If we {{7|would have checked}} a map of these differences first, we could have saved ourselves a week of work. For the second attempt, we found true north by marking the shortest shadow of a stick at midday, and we were careful to comply {{8|to}} the principal's one rule: no power tools without an adult present.

We bent a new rod to 42 degrees, aimed it at true north, and bolted it in place. On the first sunny afternoon, {{9|therefore,}} the shadow still read about an hour behind the library clock. For a moment we thought we had failed again. Then Ms. Varga reminded us that the library clock had been moved ahead an hour for daylight saving {{10|time; the sun}} had not.

passages.title: Mile Eighteen
passages.text:
Every April, about two hundred volunteers staff the water stations along the Harbor City Marathon. For the past three years, I {{1|have been}} one of them, and I have learned that handing a cup of water to a stranger who is running past is harder than it looks.

Our station sits at mile eighteen, the point where many runners begin to tire. Our captain, a retired nurse named Delia Moss, placed us in pairs in the narrow gap {{2|among}} two long tables and told us to hold each cup {{3|either by its base or to pinch it}} near the top. A cup held this way, she explained, leaves room for a runner's hand to close around {{4|it, a}} cup gripped by its rim is easily knocked away and tends to {{5|loose}} half its water.

[1] The first runners reached us at 9:40. [2] By noon our tables were sticky, our shoes were soaked, and we had handed out more than eleven thousand cups. [3] They were the elite athletes, moving so fast that most of them never slowed down. [4] Behind them came thousands of others, {{6|in various different kinds of conditions}}. {{7|}}

Around one o'clock, a runner in a faded green shirt stopped at our table, drank two cups, and {{8|asks}} whether she was still on pace to finish before the course closed. Delia checked her watch and told her yes, as long as she kept moving. The runner thanked Delia and {{9|I}} and set off again at a slow, steady jog.

I never learned whether she made it. {{10|Still,}} when the results were posted that evening, I caught myself scanning the list for a runner in a green shirt, which is not, it turns out, something a results list records.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Three Hundred Squares
passages.text:
When the Harmon Public Library turned one hundred years old last spring, the staff wanted a celebration that would {{1|evolve}} more than cake and speeches. The head librarian, Rosa Kwan, suggested a quilt. Residents who wanted to take part would each receive a plain cotton square, eight inches on a side, and decorate it however they wished{{2|; the}} library would then join the squares and hang the finished quilt in the reading room.

More than three hundred squares came back. {{3|They were all different from one another in a lot of ways.}} A retired firefighter sewed a tiny red engine onto his. A second grader drew her cat with fabric markers, giving it {{4|six legs. Because}} her cat, she explained, runs very fast.

[1] Assembling the quilt took longer than anyone expected. [2] Volunteers met every Tuesday evening for four months. [3] They laid the squares out on the floor of the community room, rearranging them until no two similar designs sat side by side. [4] Then they sewed the rows together by hand, since the library's only sewing machine {{5|could not of handled}} the thick layers where squares overlapped. {{6|}}

The finished {{7|quilt which measures}} roughly twenty feet across, now hangs above the circulation desk. Visitors often stand beneath it for several minutes, searching for {{8|there}} own square or for one made by a neighbor. {{9|}} Ms. Kwan says the quilt has done something the library has always tried to do{{10|: it}} has given hundreds of separate stories a single place to belong.

passages.title: The Box That Changed Shipping
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Lunch by Train
passages.text:
Every weekday morning in Mumbai, India, roughly five thousand delivery workers known as {{1|dabbawalas, collect}} home-cooked lunches from kitchens across the city. By lunchtime, each meal has reached its owner's desk, often many kilometers away, and by evening the empty containers are back home. The service began in the 1890s, and today it handles more than a hundred thousand lunches a day.

A single lunchbox, or dabba, usually passes through several {{2|hands. A}} collector picks it up from a home, often by bicycle, and carries it to the nearest railway station. There, the boxes are sorted {{3|by destination; then loaded}} onto commuter trains. At the other end, another worker picks them up and delivers them on foot or by handcart.

To keep track of so many boxes, the dabbawalas rely on a simple code of colors, numbers, and letters painted on each lid. The code shows where a box started, which station it is going to, and which building it must reach. Because the code is so simple, mistakes are {{4|more rarer}} than an outsider might expect.

The dabbawalas—most of whom come from farming villages outside the {{5|city, share}} their earnings within small groups and settle most problems among themselves. They use no computers or tracking devices.{{6|}} {{7|Nevertheless,}} their lunches arrive {{8|consistent}} on time, even during the city's heavy monsoon rains.

Business schools and companies around the world have studied the system, and visitors often ask to follow a lunchbox along its route. For the dabbawalas, though, the measure of success {{9|remain}} simpler: a customer whose lunch arrives warm and on time. {{10|}}

passages.title: Clearing the Glass
passages.text:
In the winter of 1902, Mary Anderson, a visitor from Alabama, rode a streetcar through New York City during a snowstorm. The driver, she noticed, could barely see. Every few minutes he {{1|opened}} the front window, reached outside, and {{2|wiping}} the snow from the glass by hand. Each time, cold air and snow blew in, and the passengers shivered.

Anderson sketched a solution {{3|before returning home; a}} rubber blade mounted outside the glass and connected to a lever inside the car. With it, a driver could clear the windshield without ever opening a window. {{4|}} In 1903 she received a patent for her "window cleaning device."

Anderson then offered the rights to her invention to a Canadian firm. The {{5|firms'}} reply, which arrived some {{6|weeks later was}} discouraging: its engineers saw no commercial value in the device. Others worried that a blade sweeping back and forth in front of a driver {{7|would end up being more of a distraction to the driver than it would end up being a help}}. In those early years of the automobile, the idea struck many people as more likely to cause accidents than to prevent them.

Anderson's patent expired in 1920 without earning her any money. By then, {{8|therefore,}} automobiles had multiplied, and mechanical wipers were becoming common. Today it is hard to imagine a car without them, though few drivers {{9|knows}} the name of the woman who first noticed what a streetcar driver could not see. {{10|}}
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Messages from the Window
passages.text:
When the engineer Washington Roebling became too ill to visit the construction site of the Brooklyn Bridge, the work did not stop. Instead, messages traveled back and forth {{1|between he}} and the site through a single person: his wife, Emily Warren Roebling.

Washington had developed a crippling illness in 1872 after working in the caissons, the pressurized chambers sunk into the riverbed to build the bridge's foundations. For years afterward he {{2|laid}} in a room overlooking the river, following the work as best he could from a distance.

Emily had no formal training as an engineer. {{3|She studied higher mathematics. She also studied the strength of materials and the construction of cables.}} Before long she could discuss the bridge's technical problems {{4|knowledgeable}} with the engineers and contractors who came to the house.

{{5|}} Some visitors assumed that the instructions she delivered were her husband's alone. Over time, however, many came to believe that Emily was making a number of the decisions herself. {{6|For example,}} the bridge kept rising: the towers were finished, the cables were spun, and the roadway was hung beneath them.

Shortly before the bridge opened on May 24, 1883, Emily Roebling {{7|was the first person to cross it by carriage before anyone else did}}{{8|. Carrying}} a rooster as a symbol of victory. Today a plaque on the bridge honors {{9|her, her husband, and his father,}} who first designed the bridge. {{10|}}

passages.title: Word-Cross
passages.text:
Most people who fill in a crossword never wonder who invented it. The answer is a British-born newspaper editor named Arthur Wynne. On December {{1|21 1913, the}} New York World printed his "Word-Cross" puzzle in its Sunday entertainment section. Wynne's grid was shaped like a diamond with an empty center, quite unlike the square grids of today's puzzles.

The puzzle caught on quickly, and readers {{2|went totally nuts for}} the new feature. Within a few weeks, a switch in the printed title had turned "Word-Cross" into "Cross-Word," and readers had begun mailing in puzzles of their own. Neither the paper's editors nor Wynne {{3|were}} prepared for how many arrived.

{{4|For about a decade, crosswords remained mostly a newspaper feature.}} Then, in 1924, two young publishers named Richard Simon and Max Schuster released a book of crossword puzzles with a pencil attached to each copy. The book {{5|did really well}}, and the success helped launch a publishing company that still exists. By the middle of the {{6|1920's}}, crosswords had become a national craze.

Not everyone was charmed. Some critics complained that the puzzles were wasting {{7|peoples'}} time, and the New York Times ran editorials that {{8|inferred}} solvers had nothing better to do.

[1] {{9|Still,}} the fad did not fade. [2] In 1942, the Times itself began publishing a crossword. [3] Its first puzzle editor, Margaret Farrar, set many of the rules that puzzle makers still follow. [4] Today, millions of people solve crosswords every day, in newspapers, in books, and on their phones. {{10|}}

passages.title: Pushing the Idea
passages.text:
{{1|Supermarkets sell many different kinds of food.}} Yet the cart was invented less than a century ago, by a grocer in Oklahoma City{{2|, Oklahoma who}} owned a chain of stores called Humpty Dumpty.

In the 1930s, shoppers carried wire or wicker baskets, and many stopped adding items {{3|being that}} the baskets grew too heavy. The grocer, Sylvan Goldman, noticed the problem. One night in 1936, the story goes, he looked at two folding chairs in his office and imagined them on wheels. With the help of a mechanic named Fred Young, he built a folding metal frame that held two baskets, one above the other.

Goldman introduced the carts in his stores in 1937, expecting shoppers to love them. {{4|To his surprise,}} the carts were {{5|almost used by no one}}. Many men said that pushing a cart made them look weak, and many women said that they had pushed enough baby carriages already.

Goldman refused to give up. He hired people to push carts around his stores and pretend to shop, and he stationed an employee at the entrance to offer each customer a cart. {{6|}} Without his persistence, shoppers {{7|might of}} kept lugging baskets for years.

{{8|Irregardless of}} the early complaints, stores across the country soon began to {{9|adapt}} the cart. Later inventors improved it; one version could slide into the cart in front of it, so carts no longer had to be folded and stored. Today carts come in many forms: small ones for children{{10|; long, narrow ones}} for crowded city stores; and motorized ones for shoppers who have trouble walking.

passages.title: The Ice King
passages.text:
Before electric refrigerators, ice in summer was a luxury in most of the world. In 1806, a young Boston merchant named Frederic Tudor set out to sell it in the tropics. He loaded a ship with about 130 tons of ice cut from New England ponds and sent it to the Caribbean island of Martinique. Much of the cargo melted before it could be sold, and {{1|much}} people in Boston laughed at the scheme.

Tudor's {{2|principle}} problem was keeping the ice frozen. On a long voyage, even thick blocks slowly {{3|evaporated}} in the ship's hold. After years of experiments, he found that packing the blocks in {{4|a certain material}} slowed melting dramatically. Within a few decades, ships carried ice to cities as far away as Calcutta, India{{5|, cut from New England ponds}}.

{{6|Ponds are common throughout New England.}} Each winter, crews marked the frozen ponds into grids, sawed out heavy blocks, and floated them to icehouses on shore. The workers {{7|theirselves}} were often farmers who needed wages during the months when their fields lay idle.

By the 1850s, ice had become an ordinary part of life in American cities. Tudor, once mocked, became known as the {{8|"Ice King," and}} his company shipped ice around the world. By the early 1900s, however, mechanical ice-making and cheaper electricity {{9|was}} steadily ending the natural-ice trade. {{10|}}

passages.title: Seventy-Two Days
passages.text:
In 1888, a young reporter for the New York World proposed a stunt: she would travel around the world faster than Phileas Fogg, the hero of Jules Verne's novel Around the World in Eighty Days. Her editors at first {{1|lead}} her to believe that a man would be sent instead, since a woman would supposedly need too much luggage. The reporter, who wrote under the name Nellie Bly, answered that if a man went, she would make the same trip for another newspaper and beat him.

On November 14, 1889, Bly boarded a steamship in New Jersey carrying a single small bag. {{2|}} She crossed the Atlantic to England and continued by train and boat to Amiens, France. When she stepped {{3|off of}} the train there, Verne and his wife were waiting to meet her. Back in New York, the World ran a contest inviting readers to guess the exact length of her trip, and a number of rival newspapers {{4|was}} following her progress.

{{5|Bly continued east across Asia.}} On the day she left, a magazine called Cosmopolitan had sent its own reporter, Elizabeth Bisland, around the world in the opposite direction. The race between Bisland and {{6|she}} drew wide attention, yet for most of the trip neither of the women knew exactly {{7|were}} the other was.

Bly arrived back in New Jersey on January 25, 1890, seventy-two days after she had left. She had {{8|beat}} Fogg's fictional record by eight days, and {{9|thousands of people jammed the station to cheer her}}. {{10|}}

passages.title: No Accident
passages.text:
{{1|Cookies are one of the most popular desserts in the United States.}} In the version most people have heard, Ruth Wakefield ran the Toll House Inn in Whitman, Massachusetts, {{2|which}} she cooked meals for travelers. One day in the 1930s, the story goes, she ran out of baking chocolate, chopped up a chocolate bar instead, and stirred the pieces into her cookie dough, expecting them to melt. They didn't, and a classic was born.

The story is charming, but historians doubt it. Wakefield was a trained dietitian and a careful cook{{3| who had written a popular cookbook}}, and the recipes she served were {{4|suppose to}} turn out the same way every time. She later said that she had set out on purpose to make something new for her guests. {{5|Because}} the accident story is appealing, it does not fit what is known about how she worked.

Whatever its origin, the cookie was an immediate hit. {{6|Lots of people liked it.}} The number of people buying Nestlé's semisweet chocolate bars {{7|were}} soon rising sharply, and the company began printing the recipe on its wrappers. Bakers who {{8|use to}} chop chocolate bars by hand were relieved when Nestlé introduced ready-made chocolate morsels in 1939.

In return for the recipe, Wakefield{{9|, reportedly,}} received a lifetime supply of Nestlé chocolate. {{10|}}

passages.title: The Third Position
passages.text:
[1] By the early 1920s, the streets of Cleveland, Ohio, were crowded with automobiles, horse-drawn wagons, bicycles, and pedestrians, all competing for the same space. [2] Some intersections had signals, but most of these could show only two commands: stop and go. [3] Because the signal switched instantly from one to the other, {{1|drivers already in the middle of an intersection had no warning that cross traffic was about to start}}.

[4] Garrett Morgan, a Cleveland inventor and businessman, had seen the danger firsthand. [5] {{2|Already known for a safety hood that firefighters and rescuers wore in smoke-filled spaces, his attention turned}} to the problem of the intersection. [6] His solution was a signal with a third position. [7] Before switching between stop and go, the signal would halt traffic in {{3|every direction, this gave}} drivers in the intersection time to clear it.

[8] Morgan received a patent for his design in 1923. [9] The signal itself was a T-shaped pole with arms that a person turned by hand, {{4|and so it}} looked little like the electric lights used today. [10] {{5|However,}} its central idea, a pause between stop and go, survives in the yellow light that appears at nearly every modern intersection.

[11] {{6|Morgan reportedly sold the rights to his signal to the General Electric Company for $40,000.}} [12] The sum allowed him to expand his other businesses, which included a newspaper and a company that made hair-care products. [13] Morgan {{7|has continued}} to work on inventions for the rest of his life, though none became as widely known as the signal.

[14] Historians are careful to note that Morgan did not invent the traffic signal; {{8|several earlier designs}} existed before his. [15] What he contributed was a solution to a specific problem that the earlier {{9|signals'}} had created. [16] {{10|In this way, his work shows how an invention can matter not because it is the first of its kind but because it fixes a flaw in what came before.}}

passages.title: Painting by Number
passages.text:
[1] In the early 1950s, Dan Robbins, a commercial artist at the Palmer Paint Company in Detroit, was looking for a way to sell more of the company's paint. [2] He remembered reading that Leonardo da Vinci had sometimes numbered sections of a sketch so that his apprentices would know which colors to apply. [3] Robbins applied the same idea to {{1|a kit, it contained}} a board printed with a numbered outline and small pots of matching paint.

[4] The company's owner, Max Klein, was doubtful at first. [5] Early kits sold poorly, {{2|because}} store owners did not know where to display them. [6] Sales {{3|improved dramatically}} after a department store demonstration showed shoppers that anyone could finish a picture in a few evenings. [7] Within a few years, Palmer was selling millions of kits a year {{4|under the name Craft Master}}.

[8] Not everyone approved. [9] Critics complained that the kits turned painting into a mechanical {{5|task; following}} instructions rather than expressing ideas. [10] {{6|To them, a picture that came with its own instructions could not really be called art.}} [11] Robbins, however, argued that the kits, along with the simple instructions included in each box, {{7|was}} a first step toward painting for many people who had never held a brush.

[12] Today, paint-by-number pictures {{8|were}} sought by collectors, including some who once dismissed them. [13] In 2001 the Smithsonian Institution held an exhibition of the paintings, presenting them as a record of how ordinary Americans {{10|spent its}} leisure time in the years after World War II.

passages.title: Bending the Light
passages.text:
[1] Before the 1820s, most lighthouses used curved metal mirrors to aim the light of their lamps out to sea. [2] Even the best mirrors wasted much of that light, and keepers spent hours each day polishing away the soot that dimmed them.

[3] The French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel, {{9|who had spent years studying how light bends,}} proposed a different {{1|approach: a lens}} that would bend the light rather than reflect it. [4] A single solid lens big enough for a lighthouse would have been {{2|extremely heavy in weight}} and difficult to cast. [5] Fresnel's solution was to divide the lens into many small glass prisms. [6] {{4|Arranged in rings around a central lens, each prism}} bent a portion of the light into one strong horizontal beam. [7] The finished lens was far lighter {{3|then}} a solid lens of the same width.

[8] In 1823 the first Fresnel lens was installed in the Cordouan lighthouse in France. {{5|}} [9] The improvement was dramatic. [10] {{6|However,}} a light that had once been visible for only a few miles could now be seen from more than twenty miles away. [11] Within a few decades, Fresnel lenses {{7|has been installed}} in lighthouses around the world, and each lighthouse's lens was chosen to suit {{8|it's}} location.

passages.title: Lines in the Sand
passages.text:
[1] In 1948, a graduate student named Bernard Silver overheard a grocery executive asking a dean at his school how stores might record a product's information automatically at the checkout. [2] Silver mentioned the problem to his friend Norman Joseph Woodland, who became fascinated by it.

[3] Woodland, who had learned Morse code as a Boy Scout, was sitting on a Florida beach {{1|when, he had an idea}}. [4] He pushed his fingers into the sand and drew them toward himself, stretching the dots and dashes of Morse code into long, thin lines. [5] Wide and narrow lines, he realized, could stand for numbers {{2|just as}} dots and dashes stood for letters.

[6] Woodland and Silver's design used circles, like a bull's-eye, so that it could be read from any direction. [7] The two received a patent for it in 1952, {{3|but}} the equipment needed to read the code was still too expensive for stores. [8] For two decades, the idea sat {{6|unused, grocers had}} no practical way to scan the codes.

[9] {{7|Lasers are also used today in medicine and in music players.}} [10] On June 26, 1974, a cashier at a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, scanned a pack of chewing gum, the first product sold using the Universal Product Code. [11] Today, barcodes {{8|is}} printed on nearly everything people buy.

passages.title: A Better Way to Fasten Boots
passages.text:
[1] In 1893, an inventor named Whitcomb Judson patented a device he called a "clasp locker." [2] It was meant to replace the long rows of buttons and hooks on high boots, {{1|but it had a serious flaw: it}} tended to pop open without warning.

[3] The problem was solved two decades later by Gideon Sundback, a Swedish-born engineer working for the company that had acquired Judson's patents. [4] {{2|Sundback's design, which used}} rows of small interlocking teeth, each shaped with a small bump on top and a matching hollow underneath. [5] A slider pressed the teeth together so that each bump nested inside the hollow of the tooth above it. [6] {{4|Increasing the number of teeth per inch, the fastener became both smaller and far more secure.}}

[7] Sundback called his invention the "hookless fastener," a name that {{5|did little to excite}} customers. [8] Sales stayed modest until 1923, when the B. F. Goodrich Company used it on a line of rubber boots. {{10|}} [9] The company's president is said to have enjoyed the sound the boots made as they were closed{{6| and he decided to call}} them "Zippers." [10] Before long, the name had spread from the boots to the fastener itself.

[11] Today, zippers close everything from jackets to tents to suitcases. [12] {{8|Few of the people who use them every day knows}} that the device began as a better way to fasten boots.
